title: CyberXero: How 51 AI Agents Helped Steal 628,000 Ukrainian Records
author: Jeanclaude Aoun
summary: A heating bill can reveal where someone lives. A subscriber database can reveal where hundreds of thousands of people live. In Kharkiv, an attacker extracted 564,073 subscriber records from a district heating provider. Names, home addresses and account numbers were among the information taken. For civilians living in a city affected by war, that exposure can have consequences far beyond fraud. The attacker operated under the name CyberXero. Its toolkit included conventional hacking software, custom scripts and 51 specialised AI agents configured through Claude Code. On 6 October 2026, SOCRadar published its investigation . Researchers reported more than 628,000 records tied to Ukrainian individuals in the attacker’s possession. This AI breach story combines automation with human-led attacks. The evidence does not establish that every agent participated in every theft. It shows how one operator assembled a powerful operation, and what happened to the information it reached. Who is CyberXero? CyberXero is a financially motivated initial access broker, according to SOCRadar. An initial access broker compromises systems and sells access to other criminals. The operation had two tracks. One targeted WordPress websites and online shops worldwide, pursuing access and payment data through automated attacks. The other focused on Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure, using carefully selected targets, detailed reconnaissance and manual exploitation. A human directed both tracks. AI agents supported tasks across reconnaissance, exploitation and activity after access was gained. The Hacker News reported that the infrastructure had been observed since July 2026. The campaign remained active when the research was published. How did CyberXero use Claude Code? Researchers found 51 specialised AI agents defined on the main workstation. These Claude Code configurations assigned different jobs: identifying targets, testing credentials, supporting exploitation and extracting data. A second layer connected the open-source testing framework PentAGI with Cobalt Strike to support payload generation and testing. The role of AI agents was to extend the operator’s capacity. Conventional tools and scripts remained central to execution. Claude Code formed part of the wider operation, rather than replacing every tool or human decision. The automated website pipeline produced striking results. According to SOCRadar, one execution: Scanned 4,708 targets . Confirmed access to 429 WordPress administration panels . Deployed 32 web shells . Completed those actions within 61 seconds . A web shell lets an attacker issue commands on a compromised server. Installing one can turn a brief intrusion into continued access. Those figures describe automated tooling within the campaign. They do not establish that AI agents independently performed every action. Did the AI agents ever refuse? Yes. The recovered logs showed refusals involving backdoors, firewall changes, movement through networks and web-shell deployment. One scan was refused four consecutive times. CyberXero repeatedly presented malicious activity as authorised security testing and restarted sessions after refusals. Some refusals held. The Claude Code session records captured attempts to push past those boundaries. They also made the human operator’s involvement visible. This matters when interpreting an AI breach: the software did not invent the criminal campaign. A person chose the objectives and kept pursuing them, using AI agents alongside established attack methods. What did CyberXero steal? SOCRadar found evidence of data theft from four Ukrainian organisations. The largest reported extraction came from the Kharkiv heating provider. A credential embedded in the attacker’s script provided direct access. An extraction tool collected 564,073 subscriber records and 213,340 access-log entries . The subscriber records included personal information, home addresses and account numbers. The logs contained timestamps and IP addresses. SOCRadar warned that exposing identifiable civilians in this setting could create physical risks. Seven additional energy-sector organisations were under reconnaissance without confirmed compromise. Behind the numbers are people who entrusted information to a service they needed. An AI breach becomes personal when those records leave the organisation responsible for protecting them. How was CyberXero discovered? CyberXero exposed its own working directory to the internet without access controls. Researchers found more than 90,000 files , including scripts containing plaintext tokens, victim database exports and session logs from AI agents. The mistake helped them map eight infrastructure nodes and reconstruct the operation. The logs documented targets, planned actions, refusals and attempted workarounds. Information collected to support the attacker’s work became evidence for researchers. What does this AI breach mean for stored files? AI agents can help an operator investigate more targets and coordinate more work. The consequences still depend on what compromised access allows. A credential with broad permissions can expose a large collection. A readable database export can concentrate thousands of customer records in one file. Contracts, identity documents and confidential reports can remain sensitive long after the work that created them is finished. Organisations need to secure their live databases. They also need to protect the copies they keep: exports, supporting documents and archives. The CyberXero investigation makes that storage question concrete. How much readable information could an attacker obtain from one compromised provider? What is Untrace Network? Untrace Network is file storage designed so that a breach of one storage provider cannot expose complete, readable documents. Each file is encrypted in your browser, then divided into six pieces, called shards, distributed across three independent providers. Rebuilding the encrypted file requires any three shards. Reading it also requires the decryption key. No single provider holds enough shards to reconstruct it. With Untrace Network, an attacker who copies one provider’s stored data obtains encrypted fragments rather than readable documents. How does Untrace Network protect your documents? Access is granted file by file. A person opens an authorised file using their passkey, with verification through their device. There is no account-wide password or server-side key that opens every file. Encryption happens before storage. Files are encrypted in the browser before leaving the device. Storage providers cannot read the documents they hold. One provider cannot reconstruct your files. Compromising a single provider does not supply enough shards to rebuild the encrypted file. Untrace Network adds protection for stored documents and exports alongside the controls your live systems need. Files opened or downloaded onto a device still depend on that device’s security. Protect your files before an AI breach You do not need to wait for an incident to reduce your exposure. Your contracts, ID scans and confidential business files deserve protection today. AI agents are becoming part of the attacker’s toolkit. Untrace Network gives you a practical way to limit what a single storage-provider breach can reveal. Try Untrace Network today. Give your important files a more protected home. Originally published at untrace.network .

title: My webhook catcher stored 100 events — then a burst of 101 deleted the one that mattered
author: InApp
summary: I built a webhook catcher for integration testing: point any sender at an ephemeral HTTPS URL, it stores up to 100 POSTs, you read them back within 24 hours. Simple. Then a retry storm happened. A third-party API was flapping, so it retried the same event dozens of times — well over my 100-event cap. My ring buffer silently overwrote the oldest entries, and the single event I actually needed to debug (a malformed payload from a specific client version) got evicted by its own retries. The bug wasn't the cap. It was that I treated "store events" and "treat events as interchangeable" as the same assumption. They aren't. A webhook catcher sees retries, duplicates, and bursts — the interesting event is often the unique one, not the latest one. The fix was boring and correct: keep the ring buffer, but fingerprint each payload (hash of body + selected headers) and maintain a separate set of "seen fingerprints." When the buffer is full, evict duplicates first; only evict unique events when nothing else is left. Also expose the fingerprint in the read-back response so I can tell "same event, retried" from "new event, same shape." I also added a per-source counter so I can see at a glance that one client sent 87 of my 100 slots. That number alone explained three "mystery" bugs in other people's test setups. Lesson: ephemeral debugging tools need the same durability thinking as production queues. If your tool's whole job is to catch the weird event, make sure a flood of normal events can't erase it. Retried webhooks are the normal case, not the edge case. It's running at https://x402.freeq.one/tools/webhook_catch.html if you want to poke at it. The 100-event cap is still there; the eviction policy just got honest.

title: Shipping Work Through a Desktop Agent: First Bot, Computer, Then Routines
author: dylan yu
summary: "AI agent" posts usually skip the boring part: how a desktop agent actually holds a computer, asks for approval, and runs again tomorrow without you re-explaining the job. If you are evaluating Grok Bot-style setups, the useful mental model is three layers — identity , computer , routines — not a chat demo. Layer 1: know what the product is (and is not) Start with a plain definition page before you install anything. What is Grok Bot is the right altitude: an agent that can use a computer and tools on your behalf, with approvals, not a magic autopilot that silently spends money and posts as you. Read that before comparison charts. Feature matrices are useless if you still think the product is "ChatGPT with a sidebar." Layer 2: first bot as a scoped employee Your first bot should have a job description, not a personality. Good first jobs are narrow: Draft a weekly changelog from merged PRs Triage inbound email into labels + draft replies you still send Watch a folder and summarize new PDFs A practical first bot path matters more than a tour of every plugin. Scope equals safety. Wide open "do whatever" agents are how people discover irreversible actions the hard way. Layer 3: the computer is the real API Chat is the interface. The computer is the capability. Files, browser, shell, and connected apps only matter if you understand what the agent can touch and what still needs your click. Skim computer with the same seriousness you would give IAM docs. Ask: Does this run on a remote box, my machine, or both? Which actions are reversible vs. externally visible? Where do approvals show up, and can a routine bypass them? If those answers are fuzzy, do not wire production credentials yet. Routines and skills turn demos into ops One-shot prompts are toys. Recurring work needs schedules, skills, and failure modes. Skills and routines is where an agent stops being a chat novelty and starts looking like a junior operator: same brief, same tools, logged outcomes. Ops hygiene that actually helps: Name the routine after the outcome ( weekly-changelog ), not the model. Keep secrets out of the prompt; use connected accounts and approvals. Log failures with the step that died (auth, timeout, empty input). Prefer read → draft → human send over silent send for anything external. For team-shaped usage, ops notes on handoff and ownership prevent the classic failure: five people sharing one bot and nobody knowing who approved the outbound message. Compare on jobs, not logos When you stack Grok Bot against other agent products, compare job completion under approval constraints , not homepage adjectives. A grounded compare page plus concrete use cases beats another "10 AI agents in 2026" listicle. Checklist before you commit a workflow: Can I state the job in one sentence? Does the agent have only the computer access that job needs? Is every externally visible action behind an approval I understand? Can the same job rerun next week as a routine without rewriting the brief? Do I know how to recover when a step sticks or a login expires? Desktop agents are less about clever prompts and more about boring operational design. Get the first bot narrow, the computer boundaries explicit, and the routine repeatable — then the chat UI finally earns its keep.
